title: Chapter 63: Soft 1
content:
Chapter 63

Soft 1

Wei Wuxian murmured in a soft, hazy daze: "...Lan Zhan."

His hand reached out, blindly catching the edge of Lan Wangji’s sleeve. Lan Wangji, who had been sitting vigil beside him the entire time, leaned down instantly. "I'm here," he whispered softly.

Wei Wuxian wasn't awake. His eyes remained sealed shut, but his grip on the fabric was fierce, clinging to him like a lifeline as he mumbled in his sleep, "...You... don’t be mad..."

Lan Wangji froze for a fraction of a second, his voice dropping into tender, uncharacteristic gentleness. "I am not angry."

"...Oh."

Reassured by the answer, his fingers slowly loosened their desperate hold.

Lan Wangji lingered by his side a moment longer. Seeing that Wei Wuxian had quieted down and was lying completely still, he moved to rise—only for Wei Wuxian’s other arm to shoot out, wrapping fiercely around his arm.

"I'll go with you!" he cried in his sleep. "Take me back to your home, hurry!"

Lan Wangji’s eyes went wide.

The sheer volume of his own shout startled Wei Wuxian awake. His long lashes fluttered, slowly parting. As the bleary fog cleared from his eyes, he suddenly registered what he was doing: he was clinging to Lan Wangji’s arm like a drowning man clutching a piece of driftwood.

He snatched his hands back so fast he nearly rolled straight off the bed. The violent jerk pulled sharply at the wound in his abdomen; a sharp gasp tore past his lips, his brows pinching in pain as memory caught up with him—right, I’m gutted. As dark spots danced across his vision, a carousel of faces spun dizzyingly through his mind: Jin Ling, Jiang Cheng, Jiang Yanli, Jiang Fengmian, Madam Yu...

Lan Wangji’s firm hand pressed down on his shoulder, keeping him still. "Your abdomen?"

Wei Wuxian grunted, "The stab wound? It's fine, doesn't hurt..."

Lan Wangji held him steady, peeling back his robes. The wound had already been cleaned and bandaged with meticulous care; loosening the linen wrap, the deep gash had astonishingly knitted itself shut without leaving a trace. Looking down at his leg, the lingering curse mark had completely vanished as well.

Wei Wuxian blinked. "How long have I been out?"

Only after double-checking that the injury was truly gone did Lan Wangji release him. "Four days."

Jin Ling’s strike had hit dead center and pierced deep; healing clean within four days without so much as a scar took nothing short of top-grade Gusu Lan celestial elixirs. Wei Wuxian offered a quiet word of thanks, then couldn't help poking fun at himself: "Look at me, coming back to life only to end up this fragile. One little poke and I’m down for the count."

Lan Wangji replied coolly, "Anyone run through by a sword would go down."

"Not necessarily," Wei Wuxian scoffed playfully. "Back in my prime, I could have had half my intestines spilling out, shoved them right back in, and fought another three hundred rounds."

Seeing him launch straight into ridiculous bravado the moment he opened his eyes, Lan Wangji shook his head, turning his face away. Terrified the man was walking out on him, Wei Wuxian blurted out, "Lan Zhan, Lan Zhan! Don't leave! I'm talking nonsense, my bad, don't ignore me!"

Lan Wangji paused. "Since when do you care if people ignore you?"

"I care, I care," Wei Wuxian said, a little breathlessly.

It had been an eternity since he’d woken up bruised and broken to find someone quietly waiting by his side.

At Lan Wangji’s waist hung two swords. Unclipping Suibian, he held the scabbard out to him. "Your blade."

Wei Wuxian froze. After a beat, he took it, murmuring, "Thank you."

Cradling the hilt, he slid the steel an inch from its sheath; the pristine, mirror-like blade reflected a pair of dark eyes right back at him. Wei Wuxian stared at his reflection for a moment, then clicked the sword back into place. "It really sealed itself?"

Lan Wangji placed his fingers around the grip and pulled. The blade refused to budge an inch, locked tight.

Wei Wuxian sighed, patting the scabbard. I knew Jin Guangyao wouldn't have the guts to fabricate something that bold on the fly... It really sealed itself. Out of all the rotten luck in the world, this miracle had to happen to me. Now the evidence is ironclad—whoever draws this sword is Wei Wuxian, no questions asked. I couldn't deny it even if I wanted to.

Glancing around, the room was sparse, immaculate, and dimly lit, save for a single paper lantern glowing softly in the corner. "Where are we?"

"The Cloud Recesses," Lan Wangji answered.

Wei Wuxian stared. "You dragged me back to the Cloud Recesses?! What if your brother catches us?"

A calm voice floated from behind a folding screen: "I already have."

The screen parted, and a figure stepped into the light. Clad in snowy robes and bearing a cloud-patterned forehead ribbon, his features were carved like flawless jade, set in a solemn, unreadable mask.

Considering he’d been resting peacefully inside the Cloud Recesses for four whole days without being dragged off in chains by the Lanling Jin Clan, Lan Xichen clearly posed no immediate threat. Besides, Lan Wangji was standing right beside him; Wei Wuxian felt no need to tense up. A sudden thought struck him, and he asked, "What happened to Chifeng-zun's remains?"

Lan Xichen replied, "The prominent clans have witnessed our brother's body with their own eyes. For now, it is in Huaisang’s custody. I have also dispatched men I trust implicitly to stand guard over it."

Wei Wuxian breathed a sigh of relief, then pressed, "And Jin Guangyao’s reaction?"

Lan Wangji’s reply was flat: "Flawless."

Wei Wuxian had fully expected Jin Guangyao to put on a masterclass in theatrics; making sure the corpse couldn't be destroyed to cover his tracks was victory enough.

Yet Lan Xichen spoke again, his tone measured and deliberate: "He declared that this matter will be investigated to the very end, and an answer will be given to the world. And now that Young Master Wei is awake... Wangji, is it not time you gave me an explanation as well?"

Lan Wangji rose to his feet. "Brother."

Lan Xichen let out a heavy, weary sigh. "Wangji... what am I supposed to say to you?"

"Brother," Lan Wangji said, his voice unyielding, "Chifeng-zun's severed head is undeniably in Jin Guangyao’s possession."

Lan Xichen looked at him. "Did you see it with your own eyes?"

"He saw it with his own eyes."

"And you believe him?"

"I do."

The answer dropped without a heartbeat of hesitation. A sudden wave of heat bloomed against Wei Wuxian's ribs.

Lan Xichen asked, "And Jin Guangyao?"

"Untrustworthy."

A wry, bitter smile touched Lan Xichen’s lips. "Wangji, on what basis do you decide who is worthy of trust and who is not?"

Turning his gaze onto Wei Wuxian, he continued, "You believe Young Master Wei, yet I believe Jin Guangyao. Neither of us witnessed our eldest brother's head in his vault with our own eyes; we are both relying on our personal understanding of another man, choosing to place our faith in his word.

"You believe you understand Wei Wuxian, so you trust him; I, too, believe I understand Jin Guangyao, so I trust him. You have faith in your own judgment—am I not permitted to trust mine?"

Fearing the conversation was on the brink of fracturing into an ugly family brawl, Wei Wuxian hurriedly cut in: "Sect Leader Lan!"

He couldn't blame Lan Xichen. Having experienced Nie Mingjue’s memories firsthand, he had seen Jin Guangyao’s venomous cruelty and ravenous ambition laid completely bare. But if Jin Guangyao had spent years wearing an impeccable mask of devotion in front of Lan Xichen, why on earth would the man doubt his own sworn brother in favor of an infamous, blood-soaked rogue who had supposedly clawed his way out of hell?

Lan Xichen dipped his chin gently. "Young Master Wei, you need not worry. Until the truth is dragged into the daylight, I will not blindly side with either party, nor will I betray your whereabouts to the clans. Had that been my intent, I would never have permitted Wangji to bring you to the Hanshi, let alone tended to your wounds myself."

Wei Wuxian bowed his head. "I thank Sect Leader Lan for giving me this chance. But Chifeng-zun's head was inside that hidden chamber—that is an absolute, undeniable fact. Not only did I lay eyes on it, but the overwhelming resentment radiating from the skull contaminated my spirit, forcing me through his memories. Does that not count as evidence?"

Lan Xichen remained remarkably poised. "Young Master Wei, you may very well have witnessed those visions. But you cannot prove that you saw them inside the private vault of Koi Tower."

Wei Wuxian clicked his tongue. "Fair point. Let us approach this from another angle, then. Chifeng-zun's direct cause of death was indeed a violent qi deviation. But doesn't Sect Leader Lan find the timing entirely too convenient? The saber spirit's curse was certainly a factor, but have you never considered that an external catalyst pushed him over the edge?"

Lan Xichen’s brow furrowed. "And what catalyst do you propose?"

"The Song of Clarity."

Lan Xichen looked at him steadily. "Young Master Wei, are you aware that the spiritual melody he played was taught to him by my own hands?"

"Then perhaps Sect Leader Lan would care to listen," Wei Wuxian offered, "and tell me if you find anything strange about it?"

His bamboo flute was resting quietly beside his pillow. Wei Wuxian picked it up, paused a moment to hum the notes in his mind, and brought the instrument to his lips. A soft, haunting melody breathed through the room. Lowering the flute, he asked, "Sect Leader Lan, is that truly the piece you imparted to Jin Guangyao?"

"It is," Lan Xichen confirmed.

Wei Wuxian was caught off guard, but he kept his composure. "What is the name of this piece?"

"It is titled Cleansing," Lan Xichen replied. "Its purpose is to pacify the heart and anchor the spiritual core."

Wei Wuxian rubbed his chin. "Cleansing... I’ve heard plenty of famous pieces from the prominent clans, so why does neither the name nor the melody ring a bell?"

Lan Wangji answered from the side, "It is obscure. And exceptionally difficult to master."

Lan Xichen nodded. "Precisely."

Wei Wuxian pressed, "Did Jin Guangyao specifically ask to learn this piece by name?"

"He did."

"If it's that notoriously difficult, why would he specifically request it instead of picking something far easier to learn?"

"Because I told him that while Cleansing is grueling to master, its healing efficacy is unmatched," Lan Xichen explained. "The phrasing is notoriously tricky—did Young Master Wei not play a passage incorrectly just now?"

A jolt ran through Wei Wuxian’s chest. "I played it wrong?"

Lan Wangji’s voice was steady: "One section in the middle was flawed."

A sharp grin split Wei Wuxian’s face. "No, no. I didn't make a mistake—Jin Guangyao did! When his spirit invaded mine, that was the exact sequence of notes he played to Nie Mingjue. I can swear on my life that I just repeated his performance note for note, without a single error."

Lan Xichen’s eyes flashed with bewilderment. "Are you suggesting he learned it improperly? That... is impossible."

"Naturally it’s impossible!" Wei Wuxian agreed. "Lianfang-zun is a brilliant mind with a terrifyingly photographic memory; how could he possibly fumble a few notes by accident? It had to be deliberate. I'll play it again. Sect Leader Lan, Hanguang-jun—please listen closely to the passage I 'played wrong'."

He lifted the flute once more. As the melody wound through the second movement, nearing its close, Lan Wangji spoke: "Stop."

Lan Xichen breathed, "That was the exact phrase."

Wei Wuxian lowered the bamboo from his lips. "Truly? But to my ears, it flowed quite naturally."

"It does flow naturally," Lan Xichen murmured grimly. "However... it is unequivocally not a part of Cleansing."

A genuine mistake in performance could never weave itself into an existing score with such seamless, organic perfection; that specific phrase had to have been meticulously ground down, polished, and stitched into the melody by design. And that alien sequence of notes—masquerading beneath the soothing guise of Cleansing—was very likely the executioner's blade that drove Nie Mingjue mad.

After a heavy silence, Lan Xichen stood. "Follow me."

Stepping out into the night, Wei Wuxian blinked in quiet surprise.

They stood before a secluded, rustic cottage tucked away in an unknown corner of the Cloud Recesses. The Lan Clan’s mountain estate was crowned by soaring pines and carpeted in lush orchids and fragrant grasses. Blossoms were rare, reserved for pale, understated blooms like white magnolias, gardenias, and chrysanthemums, used sparingly as passing accents. Yet the small yard before this cottage was smothered in a roaring sea of purple gentians. The delicate petals were intensely vivid, their rich violet hue glowing faintly under the moonlight, enchanting and dreamlike.

Wei Wuxian sensed that this place harbored a deep secret, but with no time to dwell on it, he hurried along. It was past nine; the residents of Cloud Recesses had long since retired for the night, leaving the grounds dead silent. Meeting not a single soul along the mountain paths, Lan Xichen guided them straight to the Library Pavilion.

Though the building had been reduced to ashes during the war, its reconstruction was an exact replica of the original layout, right down to the freshly planted magnolia tree standing outside the lattice windows.

Filing inside, Wei Wuxian voiced his doubt: "Sect Leader Lan, can we truly track down the origin of that melody here?"

"Not up here," Lan Xichen replied.

He strode toward a row of towering cedar bookshelves, crouched down, pulled back an woven straw mat, and lifted a concealed floorboard. "Down here, we can."

Beneath the timber lay a hidden trapdoor.

Lan Wangji murmured, "The Room of Forbidden Books."

Descending a narrow, stone-cut staircase of fifty-odd steps, a spacious, dry underground vault opened up before them, their footsteps echoing against the subterranean masonry. Rows of towering bookshelves stood in silent formation, populated sparsely by categorized tomes coated in a thick blanket of dust, undisturbed for years.

Lan Xichen led them down an aisle, gesturing toward a shelf. "This entire section houses the records of eccentric and unrecorded musical scores."

A solitary study desk sat in the center of the chamber, illuminated by a single paper lantern. Lan Wangji retrieved forgotten brushes and inkstones, smoothly transcribing three identical copies of the rogue melody from memory. Sitting around the desk, the three of them divided the labor—tackling dozens of ancient manuscripts each, turning brittle pages one by one, cross-referencing the forbidden scores to find a match.

Two hours crawled by. Not one of them turned up a single corresponding phrase. The melody had no recorded origin.

Skimming line after line of musical notation, Wei Wuxian’s thoughts churned: Is this rogue piece really absent from the Lan Clan’s forbidden archives? Impossible. If Gusu Lan doesn't possess a copy, no other sect on earth would have it. Don't tell me Jin Guangyao composed a masterwork of spiritual murder entirely from scratch? That would be a nightmare; to prove the song is lethal, we’d have to find a living subject and experiment on them for months. But brilliant as he is, he picked up cultivation late in life—he isn't a musical genius capable of inventing an entirely new discipline...

His eyes ached from the endless sea of miniature characters. With only a few scrolls left in his pile, he set them aside to rub his temples. Lan Wangji, having finished his own stack, quietly reached across the desk, gathered the scrolls Wei Wuxian had put down, and began flipping through them in silence. Lan Xichen looked up from his reading, watching the small exchange with an unreadable, hesitant flicker in his eyes.

Suddenly, Lan Wangji spoke: "This one."

He slid an open manuscript across the wood. Wei Wuxian perked up instantly, dragging the pages close to compare them against his transcribed sheet. "Wait... this looks completely different?"

Lan Wangji stood up, walked around the desk, and settled right beside him, his slender finger tapping the paper. "Look at the preceding and following pages."

Their shoulders brushed, Lan Wangji’s deep, magnetic baritone murmuring right beside his ear. Wei Wuxian’s hand gave an involuntary tremor, nearly dropping the parchment. Forcing his racing thoughts to ground themselves, he dragged his eyes away from Lan Wangji’s pale fingers and focused on the ink. "Ah... the pages before and after."

At a passing glance, the manuscript appeared completely normal. But to anyone trained in the subtle flow of spiritual music, paying close enough attention revealed a glaring fracture: the melody ending on the previous page and the melody beginning on the following page simply did not connect.
